doc.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Dime-a-dance trio jobs with Freddy Johnson and Walter Johnson
summary: Dance hall trios without bass, playing melody for dancers one or two choruses at a time.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Oh, Freddy Johnson, yes, I knew him. He lived on 99th Street. He didn’t live on San Juan Hill. Now, we got to play together quite a bit in those days, because one thing that I was always able to get were jobs in the dance halls, you know, the dime-a-dance places. Usually it was me, Freddy Johnson, and Walter Johnson, the drummer, because the trios at that time didn’t use bass players. You know, the pianists always, as I mentioned before, had a pretty sturdy left hand, and with the drummer, they just didn’t need a bass player. As a matter of fact, Teddy Wilson, who was one of the younger guys, didn’t really like a bass player. He preferred to play without a bass. But he did a lot of playing with bass players, as we know. But that . . . well, gee, as we think of it, with the Benny Goodman Quartet there was no bass player.
Yeah, or the trio, there was no bass player. That’s right. Yeah.
By this time, you must have . . . if you’re in these dance hall engagements, this required reading, I would assume.

Well, it wasn’t necessarily required, reading, but it was required knowing the tunes, no matter how you came unto them, as long as you knew the tune. But it was required playing melody. That’s what was required, you know. The dancers had to be aware of what you were playing, and that’s what got them onto the floor. Usually it was one chorus or one chorus and a half, and I think, if I remember correctly, never any more than two choruses, because, you know, it was a dime a dance, you know. [laughter] Every time you played a tune and stopped, that was another ten cents.
